sections.title: What counts as a solution: one uniform phase

board_events.text: What makes a mixture a SOLUTION?
A solution is a homogeneous mixture: same composition and properties throughout.
Single phase. Dissolved particles are below about 1 nm ($\lt$ a nanometre) $-$ too small to see, settle, or scatter light.
Two roles: the SOLVENT (larger amount) sets the physical state; the SOLUTE is what dissolves in it.
Binary solution = exactly two components. This whole chapter lives here.

segments.text: <curious> Open any kitchen and you are surrounded by solutions. So what exactly earns a mixture that name?
A solution is a homogeneous mixture. That means its composition and its properties are the same in every single sip, top to bottom.
It is a single phase. The dissolved particles are smaller than about one nanometre, far too tiny to see, to settle out, or to scatter a beam of light.
Every solution splits into two roles. The solvent is whatever is present in the larger amount, and it fixes the physical state of the whole thing. The solute is whatever dissolves into it.
When there are exactly two components, we call it a binary solution, and that is the case this entire chapter focuses on.
Here is the size picture. Below one nanometre and perfectly clear, you have a true solution.
Push the particles bigger, one to one thousand nanometres, and they start scattering light: that is a colloid. Bigger still and they settle out: that is a suspension. Neither one is a true solution.
And hold on to the headline rule: the solvent sets the state. A liquid solvent gives you a liquid solution.
<curious> Apne kitchen mein dekho, हर तरफ solutions hi solutions hain. Toh aakhir koi mixture solution kab kehlata hai?
Solution ek homogeneous mixture hota hai. Matlab uski composition aur properties हर घूँट में, ऊपर से नीचे तक, bilkul same rehti hain.
Ye single phase hota hai. Dissolved particles lagbhag one nanometre se bhi chhote hote hain, itne chhote ki na dikhein, na settle hon, na light scatter karein.
हर solution mein do roles hote hain. Solvent wo hai jo zyada amount mein hota hai, aur yahi puri solution ka physical state तय karta hai. Solute wo hai jo ismein dissolve hota hai.
Jab sirf do components hon, toh use binary solution kehte hain, aur yahi is poore chapter ka focus hai.
Ab size ki picture samjho. One nanometre se neeche aur bilkul clear, ye hai true solution.

Particles ko बड़ा karo, one se one thousand nanometre, toh ye light scatter karne lagte hain: ye colloid hai. Aur bhi बड़े hon toh settle ho jate hain: ye suspension hai. Inmein se koi bhi true solution nahi hai.
Aur main rule yaad rakho: solvent hi state तय karta hai. Liquid solvent matlab liquid solution.

board_events.caption: Solute state vs solvent state, with an anchor example in every cell

board_events.text: Name the family by the solvent: gas solvent $\to$ gaseous solution, solid solvent $\to$ solid solution.
Anchors: air (gas in gas), soda water (gas in liquid), salt water (solid in liquid).
More anchors: hydrogen in palladium (gas in solid), amalgam (liquid in solid), brass (solid in solid).
Placing a solution in its cell is the entire skill this subtopic tests.

segments.text: Let us organise every solution on a single grid.
Here is the idea that ties it all together. The solute can be a gas, a liquid, or a solid, and the solvent can independently be a gas, a liquid, or a solid.
That gives us a three-by-three grid: the state of the solute running down the side, the state of the solvent running across the top.

Look at the nine cells. Air is a gas in a gas. Soda water is carbon dioxide gas in liquid water. Salt or glucose sits as a solid in liquid water. Hydrogen tucks into palladium as a gas in a solid. An amalgam is liquid mercury in a solid metal. And brass is one solid dissolved in another.
The naming is beautifully simple. You name the family by the solvent. A gas solvent gives a gaseous solution; a solid solvent gives a solid solution.
Memorise a few anchors: air is gas in gas, soda water is gas in liquid, salt water is solid in liquid.
<whisper> And these three win you marks: hydrogen in palladium is gas in solid, an amalgam is liquid in solid, and any alloy like brass is solid in solid.
That is the whole game here: read the two states, then drop the solution into its cell.
Chalo har solution ko ek hi grid par organise karte hain.
Ye rahा wo idea jo sab kuchh jodta hai. Solute gas, liquid, ya solid ho sakta hai, aur solvent bhi independently gas, liquid, ya solid ho sakta hai.
Isse banta hai ek three-by-three grid: solute ki state side mein neeche ki taraf, aur solvent ki state upar across.

In nau cells ko dekho. Air ek gas in gas hai. Soda water carbon dioxide gas hai liquid water mein. Salt ya glucose solid ki tarah liquid water mein baithta hai. Hydrogen palladium mein gas in solid ban jata hai. Amalgam liquid mercury hai solid metal mein. Aur brass ek solid dusre solid mein ghula hua hai.
Naming बहुत simple hai. Family ka naam solvent se rakho. Gas solvent deta hai gaseous solution; solid solvent deta hai solid solution.
Kuchh anchors yaad kar lo: air gas in gas hai, soda water gas in liquid hai, salt water solid in liquid hai.
<whisper> Aur ye teen marks pakke karwate hain: hydrogen in palladium gas in solid hai, amalgam liquid in solid hai, aur koi bhi alloy jaise brass solid in solid hai.
Bas yahi hai pura khel: do states padho, phir solution ko uski cell mein daal do.

sections.title: Who is the solvent, and is it even a true solution?

board_events.text: Two rules for solvent, one test for 'true'
Different states? The one that keeps its state in the final solution is the solvent $-$ usually the liquid, or the solid framework.
Same state? The component present in the larger amount is the solvent.
In dilute aqueous ethanol water is solvent; in a trace of water in ethanol, ethanol is solvent. The role swaps with composition.

board_events.text: True solution: $\lt$ 1 nm, transparent, never settles, passes filter paper.
Colloid: 1$-$1000 nm, scatters the beam (Tyndall). Suspension: $\gt$ 1000 nm, cloudy, settles.
Only the first counts as a solution in this chapter.

segments.text: Two quick rules tell you which component is the solvent, and one test tells you whether you even have a true solution.

First, if the components are in different physical states, the solvent is the one that keeps its state in the final mixture. Usually that is the liquid, as in salt water, or the solid framework, as in an alloy.
Second, if both are in the same state, the solvent is simply the one present in the larger amount.

Here is a favourite exam twist. In dilute aqueous ethanol, water is the solvent; but in a tiny bit of water dissolved in a lot of ethanol, ethanol is the solvent. The role swaps as the composition swaps.
Now the true-solution test. Shine a torch through the liquid and watch the beam.
A true solution has particles below one nanometre. It is transparent, it never settles, and it passes clean through filter paper. The beam stays invisible.
A colloid, one to one thousand nanometres, scatters that beam so you can see it glowing: the Tyndall effect. A suspension, above one thousand nanometres, is visibly cloudy and settles on standing.
Only the first of those three is a solution in the sense of this chapter.
Do quick rules batate hain ki solvent kaun hai, aur ek test batata hai ki true solution hai bhi ya nahi.

Pehla: agar components alag physical states mein hain, toh solvent wo hai jo final mixture mein apni state बनाए rakhta hai. Aksar ye liquid hota hai, jaise salt water mein, ya solid framework, jaise alloy mein.
Doosra: agar dono same state mein hain, toh solvent bas wo hai jo zyada amount mein hai.

Ek favourite exam twist suno. Dilute aqueous ethanol mein water solvent hai; lekin thode se water mein jo bahut saare ethanol mein ghula ho, wahan ethanol solvent hai. Composition badalte hi role badal jata hai.
Ab true-solution test. Liquid mein se torch chamकao aur beam ko dekho.
True solution ke particles one nanometre se neeche hote hain. Ye transparent hota hai, kabhi settle nahi hota, aur filter paper se saaf nikal jata hai. Beam invisible rehta hai.

Colloid, one se one thousand nanometre, us beam ko scatter karta hai, isliye wo chamakta dikhता hai: yahi Tyndall effect hai. Suspension, one thousand nanometre se upar, saaf cloudy hota hai aur खड़े rehne par settle ho jata hai.
In teenon mein se sirf pehla wala is chapter ke sense mein solution hai.

segments.text: Let us classify four everyday solutions, then dodge a classic name trap.
The trick every time is the same: read the state of the solute, read the state of the solvent, and drop it into its cell.
Soda water is carbon dioxide gas dissolved in liquid water. That is gas in liquid, a liquid solution.
Brass is solid zinc dissolved in solid copper. That is solid in solid, an alloy.
A sodium amalgam is liquid mercury combined with a solid metal. The framework stays solid, so this is liquid in solid.
And the air we breathe is oxygen and other gases in mostly nitrogen. That is gas in gas, a gaseous solution.
Now the trap. German silver sounds like it contains silver, but it contains none at all. It is copper, zinc, and nickel, all solids, so it is an alloy: solid in solid.
<whisper> Here is the shortcut: the moment you read the word alloy, the answer is locked as solid in solid.
Chalo chaar everyday solutions classify karte hain, phir ek classic naam ke trap se bachte hain.
Trick har baar same hai: solute ki state padho, solvent ki state padho, aur use uski cell mein daal do.
Soda water carbon dioxide gas hai jo liquid water mein ghula hai. Ye gas in liquid hai, ek liquid solution.
Brass solid zinc hai jo solid copper mein ghula hai. Ye solid in solid hai, ek alloy.
Sodium amalgam liquid mercury hai jo solid metal ke saath mila hai. Framework solid rehta hai, isliye ye liquid in solid hai.
Aur jo hawa hum saans lete hain, wo oxygen aur baaki gases hain zyada tar nitrogen mein. Ye gas in gas hai, ek gaseous solution.
Ab trap. German silver ka naam aisा lagta hai jaise ismein silver ho, par ismein bilkul silver nahi hota. Ye copper, zinc, aur nickel hai, sab solids, isliye ye alloy hai: solid in solid.
<whisper> Shortcut ye hai: jaise hi tum alloy shabd padho, answer lock ho jata hai as solid in solid.

sections.title: Tougher cases: sublimation and 'solution vs compound'

board_events.text: Example 3 & 4: justify the classification
Ex 3: camphor slowly vanishes into sealed nitrogen gas, no liquid forms.
Solid camphor sublimes and spreads uniformly through the gas. Final phase is a gas $\to$ solid in gas.
Nitrogen is the solvent: it sets the gaseous state and is in vast excess.

board_events.text: Ex 4: is 22-carat gold a compound or a solid solution? A compound has a fixed ratio and a new identity.
An alloy forms over a range (18, 22, 24-carat); metals keep their own chemistry $\to$ variable-composition mixture.
Homogeneous, single phase, variable composition $\Rightarrow$ a solution. Gold = solvent, copper = solute.

segments.text: Two harder cases now, where you must justify the classification, not just state it.
In example three, camphor slowly disappears from a sealed jar of nitrogen, scenting the gas, while no liquid ever forms.
Solid camphor sublimes and disperses uniformly into the nitrogen. The final homogeneous phase is a gas, so this is a solid dissolved in a gas.
Nitrogen is the solvent, because it fixes the gaseous state of the mixture and is present in vast excess.
Now example four. A jeweller melts gold with a little copper to make twenty-two-carat gold. Is it a compound, or a solution? Look at the lattice.
A compound has a fixed stoichiometric ratio and a brand-new chemical identity. That is the test.
But an alloy can be made across a whole range, eighteen, twenty-two, twenty-four carat, and the metals keep their own chemistry. Copper atoms simply occupy sites in the gold lattice.
So it is homogeneous, single-phase, and of variable composition: that is a solution, not a compound. Gold is the larger amount and sets the framework, so gold is the solvent and copper the solute.
Ab do harder cases, jahan classification ko justify karna hai, sirf batana nahi.
Example teen mein, camphor dheere dheere sealed nitrogen ke jar se gayab ho jata hai, gas ko apni smell deta hai, par koi liquid kabhi nahi banta.
Solid camphor sublime hota hai aur nitrogen mein uniformly phail jata hai. Final homogeneous phase ek gas hai, isliye ye solid in gas hai.
Nitrogen solvent hai, kyunki wo mixture ki gaseous state तय karta hai aur bahut zyada excess mein hai.
Ab example chaar. Ek jeweller gold ko thode copper ke saath melt karke twenty-two-carat gold banata hai. Ye compound hai ya solution? Lattice dekho.
Compound ka ek fixed stoichiometric ratio hota hai aur ekdum naya chemical identity. Yahi test hai.

Par alloy ek poore range mein ban sakta hai, eighteen, twenty-two, twenty-four carat, aur metals apni khud ki chemistry बनाए rakhte hain. Copper atoms bas gold lattice mein sites occupy kar lete hain.

Toh ye homogeneous hai, single-phase hai, aur variable composition ka hai: yahi ek solution hai, compound nahi. Gold zyada amount mein hai aur framework banata hai, isliye gold solvent hai aur copper solute.

sections.title: Pitfalls and speed tricks for classification

board_events.text: Lock the solvent's state first
Pitfall: assuming the solvent is always water (or always the liquid). Air and alloys break that. Find the framework first.
Pitfall: 'German silver' / 'brass'. Both are alloys $=$ solid in solid, not compounds.
Pitfall: calling colloids or suspensions 'solutions'. If it scatters light or settles, it is neither.
Pitfall: mis-pairing. Always say solute-in-solvent in that order before naming the family.
Speed: lock the solvent's state first (that names the family), then the solute's state. Two reads, no calculation.
Memorise four classics: air = gas-gas, soda = gas-liquid, alloy = solid-solid, amalgam = liquid-solid.
Name it by where it lives: the solvent's state names the solution family.

segments.text: A few traps to sidestep, and one speed habit that never fails.
First trap: assuming the solvent is always water, or always the liquid. Air has a gas solvent and alloys have a solid solvent. Always find the framework or major component first.
Second trap: German silver and brass. Both are alloys, so both are solid in solid, and neither is a compound.
Third trap: calling colloids or suspensions solutions. If it scatters a beam or settles on standing, it is not a true solution.
Fourth trap: mis-pairing the states. Always say solute-in-solvent, in that exact order, before you name the family.
Now the speed habit. Lock the solvent's state first, because that alone names the family. Then read the solute's state. Two quick reads, no calculation at all.
And keep four classics on the tip of your tongue: air is gas in gas, soda is gas in liquid, an alloy is solid in solid, and an amalgam is liquid in solid.
<whisper> One line to remember it all: name it by where it lives. The solvent's state names the family.
Kuchh traps jinse bachna hai, aur ek speed habit jo kabhi fail nahi hoti.
Pehla trap: ye maan lena ki solvent hamesha water hota hai, ya hamesha liquid. Air mein gas solvent hai aur alloys mein solid solvent. Hamesha pehle framework ya major component dhundo.
Doosra trap: German silver aur brass. Dono alloys hain, isliye dono solid in solid hain, aur koi bhi compound nahi hai.
Teesra trap: colloids ya suspensions ko solution keh dena. Agar wo beam scatter kare ya खड़े rehne par settle ho, toh wo true solution nahi hai.
Chautha trap: states ko galat pair karna. Hamesha solute-in-solvent, usi exact order mein bolo, family ka naam rakhne se pehle.
Ab speed habit. Pehle solvent ki state lock karo, kyunki wahi akela family ka naam rakh deta hai. Phir solute ki state padho. Do quick reads, koi calculation nahi.
Aur chaar classics zubaan par rakho: air gas in gas, soda gas in liquid, alloy solid in solid, aur amalgam liquid in solid.
<whisper> Ek line mein sab yaad: name it by where it lives. Solvent ki state family ka naam rakhti hai.

sections.title: Why concentration needs a number, and why molarity is temperature-shy

board_events.text: Concentration: a precise how-much number
'Sweet' is useless to the next person. Concentration states exactly how much solute per given amount of solvent or solution.
Mass-based measures $-$ mass %, mole fraction, molality $-$ never change with temperature.
Mass and particle number do not change when you heat a solution.

board_events.text: Molarity is volume-based. Heat the solution, volume grows, the same moles now sit in a larger volume.
So molarity falls as temperature rises. Molality, with no volume in it, is immune.
That is why every colligative-property measurement is built on molality, not molarity.

segments.text: Before any numericals, one idea decides half your marks in this subtopic: which measures survive a change in temperature.
Calling a cup of chai sweet is useless to the next person making it. Concentration replaces that with a precise number: exactly how much solute per given amount of solvent or solution.
Here is the key split. The measures built on mass or on moles, mass percentage, mole fraction, and molality, never change when you heat or cool the solution.
The reason is simple: mass and the number of particles do not change with temperature. A gram is a gram, hot or cold.
But watch what happens to a volume-based measure. Look at the two flasks.
Molarity is moles per litre of solution. Heat the solution and it expands, so the same moles now sit in a larger volume.
A larger volume under a fixed number of moles means molarity falls as the temperature rises. Molality has no volume in it at all, so it is completely immune.
And that is exactly why every precise colligative-property measurement is built on molality, never on molarity.
Kisi bhi numerical se pehle, ek idea is subtopic ke aadhe marks tay karta hai: kaunse measures temperature change ko survive karte hain.
Chai ko sweet keh dena agle banane wale ke liye bekaar hai. Concentration uski jagah ek precise number deta hai: kitna solute per given amount of solvent ya solution.
Ye raha key split. Mass ya moles par bane measures, mass percentage, mole fraction, aur molality, kabhi nahi badalte jab tum solution ko garam ya thanda karte ho.
Wajah simple hai: mass aur particles ki number temperature se nahi badalti. Ek gram, ek gram hi rehta hai, garam ho ya thanda.
Par dekho volume-based measure ke saath kya hota hai. Do flasks dekho.
Molarity hai moles per litre of solution. Solution ko garam karo aur wo expand hota hai, isliye same moles ab ek बड़े volume mein baithte hain.
Bada volume aur fixed moles ka matlab, molarity temperature badhne par girti hai. Molality mein volume hai hi nahi, isliye wo bilkul immune hai.
Aur isi wajah se har precise colligative-property measurement molality par bani hoti hai, molarity par kabhi nahi.

sections.title: The concentration toolkit

board_events.text: Every concentration measure at a glance
Temperature-dependent: molarity only. Independent: mass %, ppm, mole fraction, molality.
Also: strength = grams of solute per litre = $M \times M_2$; for very dilute traces use ppb ($\times 10^{9}$).

segments.text: Here is the whole toolkit on one board. Do not memorise them as separate spells $-$ they are all just ratios of amount to amount.
Mass percentage is the mass of solute over the mass of the whole solution, times one hundred. It is what battery acid labels use.
Parts per million is the same ratio, but times ten to the sixth. It is for very dilute things, like fluoride or lead in drinking water.
Mole fraction is the moles of one component over the total moles, and the fractions of the two components always add to one.
Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. This is the lab favourite, because volumes are quick to pour, but it must be quoted at a stated temperature.
Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Notice the word solvent, and the word kilogram: this is the temperature-proof one.
So burn this in: only molarity changes with temperature. Mass percentage, parts per million, mole fraction, and molality all hold steady.
Two small extras: strength is just grams per litre, equal to molarity times molar mass; and for even tinier traces we use parts per billion, times ten to the ninth.
ये रहा poora toolkit ek board par. इन्हें alag-alag jaadu की तरह मत yaad karo, ये सब बस amount-to-amount ke ratios हैं।
Mass percentage hai mass of solute upon mass of the whole solution, times one hundred. Yahi battery acid ke labels use karte hain.
Parts per million wahi ratio hai, par times ten to the sixth. Ye bahut dilute cheezon ke liye hai, jaise drinking water mein fluoride ya lead.
Mole fraction hai ek component ke moles upon total moles, aur dono components ke fractions hamesha jud kar one bante hain.
Molarity hai moles of solute per litre of solution. Ye lab ki favourite hai, kyunki volumes jaldi pour ho jate hain, par ise ek stated temperature par quote karna padta hai.
Molality hai moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Solvent shabd par dhyan do, aur kilogram par: yahi temperature-proof wali hai.
तो ये पक्का yaad karo: सिर्फ़ molarity temperature से badalti है। Mass percentage, parts per million, mole fraction, और molality सब steady rehte हैं।
Do chhote extras: strength bas grams per litre hai, equal to molarity times molar mass; aur aur bhi chhote traces ke liye hum parts per billion use karte hain, times ten to the ninth.

board_events.text: Mass-based measures know nothing about volume. Only density converts mass $\leftrightarrow$ volume.
Memorise the chain, not the five formulas $-$ each one is just this chain rearranged.

segments.text: Now the single most powerful move in this subtopic: one chain that generates every interconversion you will ever need.
Always anchor on one hundred grams of solution. Then from the mass percentage you can read the grams of solute and the grams of solvent directly, with no effort.
Follow the flow. One hundred grams of solution splits into solute grams and solvent grams. Divide the solute grams by its molar mass to get moles of solute. From those moles, three branches fan out.
Divide by the solvent mass in kilograms and you get molality. In symbols, for a solution that is P percent, molality is one thousand P over one hundred minus P, all over the molar mass of the solute.
Divide instead by the volume, which you get from the density, and you get molarity: ten P d over the molar mass. That density is the piece you cannot skip.
And divide by the total moles to get the mole fraction of the solute.
Here is why density is non-negotiable. Mass-based measures know nothing about volume, and molarity is all about volume. The only quantity that turns mass into volume, or back, is density.
<whisper> So do not memorise five separate formulas. Memorise this one chain; every formula is just the chain rearranged.
अब इस subtopic का सबसे powerful move: एक chain जो हर interconversion generate karti है जो तुम्हें kabhi chahiye होगी।
Hamesha one hundred grams of solution par anchor karo. Phir mass percentage se tum seedha solute ke grams aur solvent ke grams padh sakte ho, bina kisi mehnat ke.

Flow ko follow karo. One hundred grams of solution bat-ta hai solute grams aur solvent grams mein. Solute grams ko uske molar mass se divide karo toh moles of solute milte hain. Un moles se, teen branches nikalti hain.
Solvent mass ko kilograms mein le kar divide karo toh molality milti hai. Symbols mein, P percent solution ke liye, molality hai one thousand P upon one hundred minus P, upon molar mass of solute.
Iski jagah volume se divide karo, jo tumhe density se milta hai, toh molarity milti hai: ten P d upon molar mass. Wo density wo hissa hai jise tum skip nahi kar sakte.
Aur total moles se divide karo toh solute ka mole fraction milta hai.
Density non-negotiable क्यों है, ये समझो। Mass-based measures volume के बारे में कुछ नहीं jaante, और molarity poori volume की ही baat है। सिर्फ़ density mass को volume में, या वापस, badalti है।
<whisper> Toh paanch alag formulas mat yaad karo. Ye ek chain yaad karo; har formula bas isi chain ka rearrangement hai.

segments.text: Two starter examples, and both hinge on the same habit: get to moles before you do anything else.
In example one, four grams of sodium hydroxide, molar mass forty, is dissolved to make two hundred millilitres of solution. We want the molarity.
First to moles: four over forty is zero point one zero mole. The volume is two hundred millilitres, which is zero point two zero zero litres.
Now molarity is moles over litres: zero point one zero over zero point two zero zero gives zero point five zero moles per litre. Clean.
Example two is a speed trap. Thirty-six grams of glucose in one hundred sixty-two grams of water. Look at the bar before you calculate.
Convert each to moles. Glucose is thirty-six over one hundred eighty, which is zero point two zero mole. Water is one hundred sixty-two over eighteen, which is nine point zero moles.
The mole fraction of glucose is zero point two zero over the total nine point two, which is about zero point zero two two. Tiny, because water hugely outnumbers it.
The trap is to take the ratio of the masses instead. Any option sitting near zero point one eight to zero point two zero used masses, not moles. Discard it on sight.
Do starter examples, aur dono ek hi habit par tike hain: kuchh bhi karne se pehle moles tak pahुncho.
Example ek mein, four grams sodium hydroxide, molar mass forty, dissolve karke two hundred millilitres solution banate hain. Humein molarity chahiye.
Pehle moles: four upon forty is zero point one zero mole. Volume two hundred millilitres hai, jo zero point two zero zero litres hai.
Ab molarity hai moles upon litres: zero point one zero upon zero point two zero zero deta hai zero point five zero moles per litre. Saaf.
Example do ek speed trap hai. Thirty-six grams glucose in one hundred sixty-two grams water. Calculate karne se pehle bar dekho.
Har ek ko moles mein badlo. Glucose hai thirty-six upon one hundred eighty, jo zero point two zero mole hai. Water hai one hundred sixty-two upon eighteen, jo nine point zero moles hai.
Glucose ka mole fraction hai zero point two zero upon total nine point two, jo lagbhag zero point zero two two hai. Bahut chhota, kyunki water uski संख्या se bahut zyada hai.
Trap ye hai ki masses ka ratio le lo. Koi bhi option jo zero point one eight se zero point two zero ke paas ho, usne masses use kiye, moles nahi. Use dekhte hi discard karo.

segments.text: Now the two examples that decide exam marks: a full interconversion, and a dilution.

Example three: a fifteen percent by weight urea solution, molar mass sixty, density one point zero five. Anchor on one hundred grams. That gives fifteen grams of urea, which is zero point two five mole, and eighty-five grams, or zero point zero eight five kilograms, of water.

For molarity, first get the volume from the density: one hundred over one point zero five is ninety-five point two four millilitres. Then molarity is zero point two five over zero point zero nine five two four, about two point six three moles per litre.
For molality, use the solvent mass directly: zero point two five over zero point zero eight five, about two point nine four moles per kilogram.
Notice molality came out larger than molarity here. That is typical for aqueous solutions, because the solvent mass in kilograms is a smaller number than the solution volume in litres.
Example four is concentrated sulphuric acid, ninety-eight percent, density one point eight four. Watch the dilution picture: the same acid particles just spread through more water.
First the stock molarity, straight from the chain: ten times ninety-eight times one point eight four, over ninety-eight, which is eighteen point four moles per litre.

<whisper> Then dilution conserves moles, so molarity one times volume one equals molarity two times volume two. Eighteen point four times V one equals zero point five zero times one thousand millilitres, giving about twenty-seven millilitres of concentrated acid, added carefully into water.
Ab wo do examples jo exam marks tay karte hain: ek poora interconversion, aur ek dilution.

Example teen: pandrah percent by weight urea solution, molar mass sixty, density one point zero five. One hundred grams par anchor karo. Isse milte hain fifteen grams urea, jo zero point two five mole hai, aur eighty-five grams, yaani zero point zero eight five kilograms, water.

Molarity ke liye, pehle density se volume nikalo: one hundred upon one point zero five is ninety-five point two four millilitres. Phir molarity hai zero point two five upon zero point zero nine five two four, lagbhag two point six three moles per litre.
Molality ke liye, seedhा solvent mass use karo: zero point two five upon zero point zero eight five, lagbhag two point nine four moles per kilogram.
Dhyan do molality yahan molarity se badi aa gayi. Ye aqueous solutions mein typical hai, kyunki solvent mass kilograms mein solution volume litres se chhota number hota hai.
Example chaar hai concentrated sulphuric acid, ninety-eight percent, density one point eight four. Dilution picture dekho: wahi acid particles bas zyada water mein phail jate hain.
Pehle stock molarity, seedha chain se: ten times ninety-eight times one point eight four, upon ninety-eight, jo eighteen point four moles per litre hai.

<whisper> Phir dilution moles ko conserve karta hai, toh molarity one times volume one equals molarity two times volume two. Eighteen point four times V one equals zero point five zero times one thousand millilitres, jo deta hai lagbhag twenty-seven millilitres concentrated acid, dhyaan se paani mein daala hua.

sections.title: Concentration pitfalls and speed anchors

board_events.text: Write down solvent vs solution before substituting
Pitfall: thinking molarity is temperature-proof. It is not $-$ volume expands, so molarity falls on heating.
Pitfall: solvent vs solution. Molality uses solvent MASS; molarity uses solution VOLUME; mass % uses solution MASS.
Pitfall: forgetting density on any molarity to molality (or % to molarity) conversion.
Pitfall: mole fraction from raw masses. Always convert to moles first.
Speed: given a mass %, anchor on 100 g and everything falls out. For dilution, jump straight to $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$.
Sanity: for dilute aqueous solutions, molality and molarity are numerically close (1 L $\approx$ 1 kg water).
molality = Mass of solvent (temp-proof); Molarity = voluMe of solution (temp-shy).

segments.text: Four traps, and two anchors that speed everything up.
First trap: thinking molarity is temperature-proof. It is not. Volume expands with heat, so molarity falls. Only the mass and mole based measures hold steady.

Second trap: solvent versus solution. Molality uses the mass of the solvent; molarity uses the volume of the solution; mass percentage uses the mass of the solution. Write down which one before you substitute.
Third trap: forgetting density. Any conversion between molarity and molality, or between mass percentage and molarity, needs the density as the bridge.
Fourth trap: taking a mole fraction from raw masses. Always convert to moles first, never ratio the masses.

Now the speed anchors. Whenever you are given a mass percentage, anchor on one hundred grams and the solute grams, solvent grams, and volume all fall out at once. For any dilution, skip the derivation and go straight to molarity one volume one equals molarity two volume two.

And a sanity check: for dilute aqueous solutions, molality and molarity come out numerically close, because one litre of dilute solution is about one kilogram of water. A big gap between them signals an arithmetic slip.
<whisper> One mnemonic ties it up: molality is Mass of solvent and temperature-proof; Molarity is voluMe of solution and temperature-shy.
Chaar traps, aur do anchors jo sab kuchh तेज़ kar dete hain.
Pehla trap: ye sochna ki molarity temperature-proof hai. Nahi hai. Volume garmi se expand hota hai, isliye molarity girti hai. Sirf mass aur mole based measures steady rehte hain.
Doosra trap: solvent versus solution. Molality solvent ki mass use karti hai; molarity solution ka volume; mass percentage solution ki mass. Substitute karne se pehle likh lo kaunsा wala hai.
Teesra trap: density bhoolna. Molarity aur molality ke beech, ya mass percentage aur molarity ke beech koi bhi conversion, density ko bridge ki tarah maangta hai.
Chautha trap: raw masses se mole fraction lena. Hamesha pehle moles mein badlo, masses ka ratio kabhi mat lo.

Ab speed anchors. Jab bhi mass percentage diya ho, one hundred grams par anchor karo aur solute grams, solvent grams, aur volume sab ek saath nikal aate hain. Kisi bhi dilution ke liye, derivation chhodo aur seedha molarity one volume one equals molarity two volume two par jao.

Aur ek sanity check: dilute aqueous solutions ke liye, molality aur molarity numerically paas aati hain, kyunki one litre dilute solution lagbhag one kilogram water hai. Dono mein बड़ा gap arithmetic slip ka signal hai.
<whisper> Ek mnemonic sab baandh deta hai: molality hai Mass of solvent aur temperature-proof; Molarity hai voluMe of solution aur temperature-shy.

board_events.text: Solubility = how much fits, at equilibrium

board_events.text: That steady busy balance is dynamic equilibrium $-$ the heart of dissolving.
A saturated solution is in equilibrium with undissolved solute; it holds the maximum at that temperature and pressure.
Solubility = the concentration of solute in that saturated solution. Below the max it is unsaturated.
Solubility is a relationship, not a fixed trait: 'like dissolves like'. Sugar in water; sulphur in carbon disulphide.
Match the intermolecular forces (polarity) and dissolution happens.

segments.text: <curious> What does it really mean to say a substance is soluble, and how much is 'how much'? It all starts with a balance.
Picture a packed Mumbai local at rush hour. People keep pushing in, and an equal number keep spilling out at every stop, so the crowd inside the compartment stops changing.
That is exactly the picture at the surface of a liquid. Gas molecules enter the liquid and leave it, and at balance the two rates are equal.
Chemists call that steady, busy balance a dynamic equilibrium, and it is the very heart of dissolving.
A saturated solution sits in equilibrium with undissolved solute. It holds the maximum amount it possibly can at that temperature and that pressure.
The concentration of solute in that saturated solution is its solubility. Add a little less and there is still room: that is unsaturated.

And solubility is not a fixed personality trait. It is a relationship between solute, solvent, and conditions. The old kitchen rule captures it: like dissolves like. Sugar vanishes into water; sulphur prefers carbon disulphide.
So the trick is simple: match the intermolecular forces, the polarities, and dissolution happens.
<curious> Kisi substance ko soluble kehne ka asli matlab kya hai, aur 'kitna' kitna hota hai? Sab kuchh ek balance se shuru hota hai.
Ek packed Mumbai local rush hour mein socho. Log andar ghuste rehte hain, aur utne hi log हर stop par bahar nikalte rehte hain, isliye compartment ke andar ki bheed badalna band ho jati hai.
Yahi picture liquid ki surface par hai. Gas molecules liquid mein enter karte hain aur bahar nikalte hain, aur balance par dono rates barabar ho jati hain.
Chemists is steady, busy balance ko dynamic equilibrium kehte hain, aur yahi dissolving ka असली dil hai.
Ek saturated solution undissolved solute ke saath equilibrium mein baithta hai. Wo us temperature aur us pressure par maximum amount rakhta hai jo rakh sakta hai.
Us saturated solution mein solute ki concentration hi uski solubility hai. Thoda kam daalo toh अभी jagah baaki hai: wo unsaturated hai.

Aur solubility koi fixed personality trait नहीं hai. Ye solute, solvent, aur conditions ke beech ka rishta hai. Purana kitchen rule ise pakadta hai: like dissolves like. Sugar water mein gayab ho jata hai; sulphur carbon disulphide ko pasand karta hai.
Toh trick simple hai: intermolecular forces, polarities ko match karo, aur dissolution ho jata hai.

board_events.text: Compress the gas: more molecules per unit volume strike the surface, so more enter than leave $-$ solubility rises with pressure.
This is Henry's story: double the pressure of CO2 over a cold drink and you roughly double how much dissolves.
Open the bottle: pressure drops, dissolved gas rushes out $-$ the fizz.
Now temperature. Dissolving a gas is like a mini-condensation: it releases heat, so it is exothermic.
Write it as gas + liquid $\rightleftharpoons$ solution + heat. Adding heat shifts it backward (Le Chatelier), expelling gas.
So gas solubility FALLS as temperature rises: warm soda goes flat; fish prefer cold, oxygen-rich water.

segments.text: For gases, two dials matter, and they pull in opposite directions. Get this asymmetry and you own the subtopic.
Look at the two cylinders. Left is a gas at low pressure over a liquid, with only a few dissolved dots. Right is the same gas compressed to high pressure.

When you compress the gas, you pack more molecules into the space above the liquid. More of them strike and enter the surface, so entering beats leaving until a new balance forms with more gas dissolved. Solubility rises with pressure.
That is Henry's whole story in words: double the pressure of carbon dioxide over a cold drink, and you roughly double how much dissolves.
Release that pressure by opening the bottle, and the dissolved gas rushes straight back out. That is the fizz.
Now the other dial, temperature. Dissolving a gas is like a tiny condensation: the molecules settle into the liquid and release heat, so it is exothermic.
Write the balance as gas plus liquid gives solution plus heat. By Le Chatelier's principle, adding heat pushes that equilibrium backward, expelling dissolved gas.
So gas solubility falls as temperature rises. That is why warm soda goes flat, and why fish are happier in cold water, which holds more dissolved oxygen.
Gases ke liye do dials matter karte hain, aur wo opposite directions mein khinchte hain. Is asymmetry ko samjho aur ye subtopic tumhara hai.
Do cylinders dekho. Left mein gas low pressure par liquid ke upar hai, sirf kुछ dissolved dots ke saath. Right mein wahi gas high pressure par compress kiya gaya hai.

Jab tum gas compress karte ho, tum liquid ke upar ki jagah mein zyada molecules bhar dete ho. Un mein se zyada surface par takra kar enter karte hain, isliye entering leaving se aage nikal jata hai jab tak ek naya balance na bane, zyada gas dissolved ke saath. Solubility pressure ke saath badhti hai.
Yahi Henry ki poori kahani hai shabdon mein: cold drink ke upar carbon dioxide ka pressure double karo, aur jitna dissolve hota hai wo lagbhag double ho jata hai.
Bottle khol kar wo pressure release karo, aur dissolved gas seedha wapas bahar nikal jati hai. Yahi fizz hai.
Ab doosra dial, temperature. Gas ko dissolve karna ek chhoti condensation jaisa hai: molecules liquid mein baith kar heat release karte hain, isliye ye exothermic hai.
Balance ko aise likho: gas plus liquid deta hai solution plus heat. Le Chatelier's principle se, heat daalne par ye equilibrium peeche shift hota hai, dissolved gas ko bahar nikalta hai.
Toh gas solubility temperature badhne par girti hai. Isiliye warm soda flat ho jata hai, aur fish cold water mein zyada khush hoti hain, jo zyada dissolved oxygen rakhta hai.

board_events.text: Endothermic dissolving (most solids): heat shifts it forward, so solubility rises with temperature.
NaNO3 climbs steeply; NaCl is near-flat (tiny enthalpy); Na2SO4 rises then falls past 32.4 C as the hydrate gives way.
There is no universal rule: the SIGN of the dissolution enthalpy decides the direction.
Pressure barely touches solids or liquids $-$ they are nearly incompressible.
Chemistry also sets a baseline: easily-liquefied gases (CO2, NH3) dissolve more than 'permanent' gases (H2, He).
Salting-out: dissolved electrolytes (and sugar) lower gas solubility $-$ a gas is less soluble in salt water.

segments.text: Solids play by different rules, and this graph tells the whole story.
The axes are solubility against temperature. Watch three real salts behave completely differently.
For a solid whose dissolving is endothermic, which is most solids, adding heat shifts the equilibrium forward, so solubility rises with temperature.

Sodium nitrate climbs steeply. Sodium chloride is almost flat, because its dissolution enthalpy is near zero, which is why salt behaves much the same in hot or cold water. Sodium sulphate is the trickster: it rises up to about thirty-two point four degrees Celsius, then falls, because a hydrate gives way to the anhydrous salt.
So burn this in: there is no universal rule. The sign of the dissolution enthalpy decides the direction, up or down.
Pressure, meanwhile, barely touches solids or liquids at all, because they are nearly incompressible. Squeezing them changes almost nothing.

Chemistry also sets a baseline before temperature and pressure even speak. Easily-liquefied gases like carbon dioxide and ammonia dissolve far more readily than permanent gases like hydrogen or helium, because they bring stronger attractions.

And one more that examiners love: salting-out. Dissolved electrolytes, and even sugar, lower gas solubility. A gas is less soluble in salt water than in pure water, because the ions grab the water molecules first.
Solids alag rules se khelte hain, aur ye graph poori kahani batata hai.
Axes hain solubility against temperature. Teen real salts ko bilkul alag-alag behave karte dekho.
Jis solid ka dissolving endothermic hai, jo zyadatar solids hain, heat daalne par equilibrium aage shift hota hai, isliye solubility temperature ke saath badhti hai.

Sodium nitrate steeply chadhta hai. Sodium chloride lagbhag flat hai, kyunki uski dissolution enthalpy near zero hai, isiliye salt garam ya thande paani mein lagbhag same behave karta hai. Sodium sulphate trickster hai: ye lagbhag thirty-two point four degrees Celsius tak chadhta hai, phir girta hai, kyunki ek hydrate anhydrous salt ko jagah de deta hai.
Toh ye pakka yaad rakho: koi universal rule नहीं hai. Dissolution enthalpy ka sign direction tay karta hai, upar ya neeche.
Pressure, वहीं, solids ya liquids ko lagbhag chhuता hi नहीं, kyunki wo nearly incompressible hain. Unhein dabane se lagbhag kuchh nahi badalta.

Chemistry bhi ek baseline set kar deti hai temperature aur pressure ke bolne se pehle. Easily-liquefied gases jaise carbon dioxide aur ammonia permanent gases jaise hydrogen ya helium se kahin zyada aasani se dissolve hote hain, kyunki wo stronger attractions laate hain.

Aur ek aur jo examiners ko pasand hai: salting-out. Dissolved electrolytes, aur sugar bhi, gas solubility ko kam karte hain. Gas salt water mein pure water se kam soluble hai, kyunki ions pehle water molecules ko pakad lete hain.

board_events.text: p = K_H x, and what K_H really tells you

board_events.text: Since x is dimensionless, K_H carries the units of pressure (Pa, bar, kbar). And K_H rises with temperature.
For 'find x': divide p by K_H. For 'new solubility at new pressure': use the ratio $-$ skip K_H entirely.

segments.text: Now the one equation that quantifies everything we just reasoned out, plus the single most examined inference from it.
Henry's law: the partial pressure p of a gas above the solution equals a constant K sub H times x, the mole fraction of gas dissolved.
So p is the pressure of the gas sitting above the liquid, and x is how much has dissolved, measured as a mole fraction. That x is our solubility.
On a graph of p against x it is a straight line through the origin, and its slope is K sub H. Look at the two lines: the steeper one has the larger K sub H.
Rearrange to x equals p over K sub H, and the key inference jumps out: at a given pressure, a larger K sub H forces a smaller x. K sub H and solubility are inversely related.

Two quick facts. Because x is dimensionless, K sub H must carry the units of pressure. And K sub H rises with temperature, which is just another way of saying gas solubility falls when the liquid warms.
One more handy tool. At constant temperature, since solubility is proportional to pressure, the ratio s one over s two equals p one over p two.
<whisper> So two shortcuts: to find x, just divide p by K sub H; and to find a new solubility at a new pressure, use that ratio and skip computing K sub H altogether.
Ab wo ek equation jo abhi jo humne reason kiya use quantify karti hai, plus usse निकला sabse zyada examine hone wala inference.
Henry's law: gas ka partial pressure p solution ke upar equals ek constant K sub H times x, gas ka dissolved mole fraction.
Toh p wo pressure hai jo gas liquid ke upar baitha hai, aur x hai kitna dissolve hua, mole fraction mein mapa gaya. Wahi x hamari solubility hai.
p against x ke graph par ye origin se jaati ek straight line hai, aur uska slope K sub H hai. Do lines dekho: jo steeper hai uska K sub H bada hai.
Rearrange karke x equals p over K sub H, aur key inference saamne aa jata hai: ek given pressure par, bada K sub H chhota x majboor karta hai. K sub H aur solubility inversely related hain.

Do quick facts. Kyunki x dimensionless hai, K sub H ko pressure ke units carry karne padte hain. Aur K sub H temperature ke saath badhta hai, jo bas doosre tareeke se kehna hai ki gas solubility liquid garam hone par girti hai.
Ek aur handy tool. Constant temperature par, kyunki solubility pressure ke proportional hai, ratio s one over s two equals p one over p two.
<whisper> Toh do shortcuts: x nikalne ke liye, bas p ko K sub H se divide karo; aur naye pressure par nayi solubility ke liye, us ratio ko use karo aur K sub H compute karna poora skip karo.

segments.text: Two examples: one plugs into Henry's law, the other tests whether you truly understand the inverse rule.

Example one, board level. At two hundred ninety-three kelvin, oxygen sits at zero point eight zero bar over water, and K sub H is thirty-five kilobar, which is thirty-five thousand bar. Find the dissolved mole fraction.
Straight from the law: x equals p over K sub H, which is zero point eight zero over thirty-five thousand, giving two point three times ten to the minus five.
Notice how a huge K sub H forces a tiny x. Oxygen is only sparingly soluble. And the one thing you must not slip on: keep p and K sub H in the same pressure unit before dividing.

Example two is a speed trap. Four gases with K sub H values of zero point four zero, one point seven, forty, and one hundred forty-five kilobar. Order them by increasing solubility, and do not compute anything.
Just use the inverse rule. Larger K sub H means smaller solubility, so increasing solubility means decreasing K sub H. Read the bars from tallest to shortest.
So increasing solubility runs S, then R, then Q, then P, exactly the reverse of the K sub H order.
<whisper> The elimination trick: any option that calls the biggest K sub H gas the most soluble is wrong the instant you see it.
Do examples: ek Henry's law mein plug karta hai, doosra test karta hai ki tum sach mein inverse rule samajhte ho ya nahi.

Example ek, board level. Two hundred ninety-three kelvin par, oxygen zero point eight zero bar par water ke upar baitha hai, aur K sub H hai thirty-five kilobar, jo thirty-five thousand bar hai. Dissolved mole fraction nikalo.
Seedha law se: x equals p over K sub H, jo zero point eight zero over thirty-five thousand hai, deta hai two point three times ten to the minus five.

Dhyan do kaise ek huge K sub H ek tiny x majboor karta hai. Oxygen sirf sparingly soluble hai. Aur ek cheez jispar slip nahi karni: divide karne se pehle p aur K sub H ko same pressure unit mein rakho.

Example do ek speed trap hai. Chaar gases K sub H values zero point four zero, one point seven, forty, aur one hundred forty-five kilobar ke saath. Inhein increasing solubility se order karo, aur kuchh compute mat karo.
Bas inverse rule use karo. Bada K sub H matlab chhoti solubility, toh increasing solubility matlab decreasing K sub H. Bars ko sabse ऊँचे se sabse chhote tak padho.
Toh increasing solubility chalti hai S, phir R, phir Q, phir P, bilkul K sub H order ka ulta.
<whisper> Elimination trick: koi bhi option jo sabse bade K sub H gas ko sabse soluble kahe, wo dekhte hi galat hai.

segments.text: The two big examples: turning a mole fraction into a real mass, and splitting a gas mixture by its partial pressures.
Example three. Carbon dioxide sits at four point zero bar over five hundred millilitres of water, with K sub H one point six times ten cubed bar. We want the mass of carbon dioxide dissolved.

First the mole fraction: four point zero over one point six times ten cubed is two point five times ten to the minus three. Then the moles of water: five hundred grams over eighteen is twenty-seven point eight moles.

For a dilute solution, x is roughly the moles of gas over moles of water, so moles of carbon dioxide is x times twenty-seven point eight, about six point nine four times ten to the minus two. Times the molar mass forty-four gives about three point one grams. Open the cap and most of that escapes as fizz.
Example four brings in Dalton. The key insight: Henry's law applies to each gas independently, using its own partial pressure.

Dry air at five point zero bar is seventy-nine percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen. So the partial pressures are three point nine five bar and one point zero five bar. K sub H is seventy-six kilobar for nitrogen and thirty-five kilobar for oxygen.
The dissolved ratio is each partial pressure over its own K sub H. That works out to about one point seven three to one.

Here is the punchline. In the air the ratio is nearly three point seven six, but dissolved it falls to one point seven three. The water is comparatively enriched in oxygen, because oxygen has the smaller K sub H. That is exactly why dissolved oxygen, not nitrogen, sustains aquatic life.

sections.title: Pitfalls and speed tricks for Henry's law

board_events.text: Never read a big K_H as 'more soluble'
Pitfall: inverting the K_H rule. High K_H = stubborn, LOW-solubility gas. Mnemonic: high K, gas wants to eKscape.
Pitfall: applying the solid temperature-trend to gases. Heating dissolves more solid, but expels gas.
Pitfall: unit mismatch. K_H is often in kbar while p is in bar $-$ convert, or you are off by a factor of a thousand.
Pitfall: treating x as a concentration. x is a mole fraction $-$ multiply by moles of solvent to reach moles or mass.
Speed: to compare/order solubility, just rank K_H and flip it. For new pressure, use s1/s2 = p1/p2.
Sanity: dissolved gas mole fractions are tiny, around $10^{-5}$. If x comes out near 1, you divided wrong.
Law fails when: pressure too high, temperature too low, or the gas reacts (NH3, HCl, O2 in blood).

segments.text: Four traps, then the shortcuts and a sanity check.
First trap, the big one: inverting the K sub H rule. A high K sub H is a stubborn, low-solubility gas. The mnemonic: high K, the gas wants to escape.
Second trap: applying the solid temperature-trend to gases. Heating dissolves more of most solids, but it expels a gas. Anchor it with warm soda going flat.
Third trap: unit mismatch. K sub H is often quoted in kilobar while the pressure is given in bar. Convert first, or your answer is off by a factor of a thousand.
Fourth trap: treating x as a concentration. It is a mole fraction. To reach moles or mass you must multiply by the moles of solvent and use molar masses.

Now the speed moves. To compare or order solubility, never plug numbers: just rank the K sub H values and flip the order. For a new solubility at a new pressure, use the ratio s one over s two equals p one over p two.
And a sanity check: dissolved gas mole fractions are tiny, around ten to the minus five. If your x comes out anywhere near one, you almost certainly divided by the wrong quantity.
<whisper> Finally, remember when the law breaks: pressure too high, temperature too low, or the gas reacts with the solvent, like ammonia, hydrogen chloride, or oxygen binding to blood.
Chaar traps, phir shortcuts aur ek sanity check.
Pehla trap, sabse bada: K sub H rule ko invert karna. Bada K sub H ek stubborn, low-solubility gas hai. Mnemonic: high K, gas escape karna chahti hai.
Doosra trap: solid temperature-trend ko gases par lagana. Heating zyadatar solids ko zyada dissolve karti hai, par gas ko bahar nikaalti hai. Ise warm soda flat hone se anchor karo.
Teesra trap: unit mismatch. K sub H aksar kilobar mein quote hota hai jabki pressure bar mein diya hota hai. Pehle convert karo, warna answer ek thousand ke factor se galat hoga.
Chautha trap: x ko concentration samajhna. Ye ek mole fraction hai. Moles ya mass tak pahुnchne ke liye ise moles of solvent se multiply karo aur molar masses use karo.

Ab speed moves. Solubility compare ya order karne ke liye, kabhi numbers plug mat karo: bas K sub H values ko rank karo aur order flip karo. Naye pressure par nayi solubility ke liye, ratio s one over s two equals p one over p two use karo.
Aur ek sanity check: dissolved gas mole fractions bahut chhote hote hain, lagbhag ten to the minus five. Agar tumhara x kahin one ke paas aata hai, toh tumne galat quantity se divide kiya hai.

<whisper> Aakhir mein, yaad rakho law kab tootta hai: pressure bahut high, temperature bahut low, ya gas solvent ke saath react kare, jaise ammonia, hydrogen chloride, ya oxygen jo blood se bind hoti hai.

Picture a packed train door: swap some passengers for stationary luggage and fewer can jump out each stop.

segments.text: <curious> Why does dropping sugar into water quietly change how the water evaporates? It starts with vapour pressure.

Picture a sealed steel tiffin, half full of water. Surface molecules with enough energy escape into the space above, and vapour molecules fall back in. Very soon the two rates match: a dynamic equilibrium, the same balance we met with dissolving gases.
The pressure exerted by that vapour, sitting in equilibrium above its own liquid, is the liquid's vapour pressure. Petrol has a high one; glycerine a low one.
Now watch the surface as we add solute. Look at the two beakers.
Stir in a non-volatile solute like sugar. It has no desire to evaporate, but it does sit on the surface, occupying spots that used to be water.
With fewer solvent molecules lining the surface, fewer escape each second, so the vapour pressure of the solution drops below that of pure water.
So a non-volatile solute always lowers the solvent's vapour pressure, and the more solute particles crowd the surface, the greater the drop.
Picture the doorway of a packed train. Replace some would-be passengers with stationary luggage, and fewer people can jump out at each stop. That is the escape rate falling.

Ek sealed steel tiffin socho, aadha water se bhara. Surface ke molecules jinke paas kaafi energy hai upar ki jagah mein escape karte hain, aur vapour molecules wapas gir jate hain. Bahut jaldi dono rates match ho jaati hain: ek dynamic equilibrium, wahi balance jo humne dissolving gases mein dekha tha.
Wo vapour jo apne hi liquid ke upar equilibrium mein baitha hai, uska pressure hi liquid ka vapour pressure hai. Petrol ka high hota hai; glycerine ka low.
Ab surface ko dekho jaise hum solute daalte hain. Do beakers dekho.
Ek non-volatile solute jaise sugar daalo. Use evaporate karne ki koi ichchha nahi, par wo surface par baithta hai, un spots ko ghere jo pehle water the.

Ek packed train ka darwaza socho. Kuchh would-be passengers ki jagah stationary luggage rakh do, aur हर stop par kam log bahar kood sakte hain. Yahi escape rate ka girna hai.

A-B stronger (new H-bonds): molecules held back, VP runs low $\Rightarrow$ negative deviation.
Push a deviation far enough and you get an azeotrope: identical liquid and vapour composition.
Positive $\to$ minimum-boiling azeotrope; negative $\to$ maximum-boiling. That is why ethanol stalls near 95%.

segments.text: Some mixtures obey Raoult's law perfectly; most misbehave. The reason is entirely about which molecules attract which.
Raoult's picture is that each volatile component contributes vapour in proportion to its own mole fraction, exactly like the doorway idea.

A solution that obeys this across the whole composition range is called ideal. That happens when the new solute-solvent attractions are about as strong as the original attractions each liquid had for itself.
Real mixtures bow away from the ideal straight line. Look at the two plots.
If the A-B attractions are weaker than the average, molecules escape more easily, so the vapour pressure runs above the ideal line. That is a positive deviation.
If the A-B attractions are stronger, often because a new hydrogen bond forms on mixing, molecules are held back, so the vapour pressure runs below the line. That is a negative deviation.
Push either deviation far enough and you reach an azeotrope, a mixture that boils at a constant temperature with identical liquid and vapour compositions.

The mapping matters: a large positive deviation gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope, and a large negative one gives a maximum-boiling azeotrope. That minimum-boiling case is exactly why you cannot push ethanol past about ninety-five percent by ordinary distillation.
Kuchh mixtures Raoult's law ko perfectly maante hain; zyadatar misbehave karte hain. Wajah poori tarah is baare mein hai ki kaunse molecules kise attract karte hain.
Raoult ki picture ye hai ki har volatile component apne mole fraction ke proportion mein vapour deta hai, bilkul doorway wale idea ki tarah.

Jo solution ise poore composition range mein maane use ideal kehte hain. Ye tab hota hai jab naye solute-solvent attractions lagbhag utne hi strong hon jitne har liquid ke apne liye original attractions the.
Real mixtures ideal straight line se hatt kar jhukte hain. Do plots dekho.
Agar A-B attractions average se weaker hain, molecules zyada aasani se escape karte hain, toh vapour pressure ideal line ke upar chalta hai. Ye positive deviation hai.
Agar A-B attractions stronger hain, aksar isliye ki mixing par ek naya hydrogen bond banta hai, molecules ruk jate hain, toh vapour pressure line ke neeche chalta hai. Ye negative deviation hai.
Kisi bhi deviation ko kaafi door tak push karo aur tum ek azeotrope tak pahुnchte ho, ek mixture jo constant temperature par boil karta hai identical liquid aur vapour compositions ke saath.

Mapping matter karti hai: bada positive deviation minimum-boiling azeotrope deta hai, aur bada negative maximum-boiling azeotrope. Wahi minimum-boiling case exactly wajah hai ki tum ethanol ko ordinary distillation se lagbhag ninety-five percent se aage nahi le ja sakte.

segments.text: Now the formulas. There are two Raoult forms, and the single most common mistake in this whole subtopic is mixing them up.
First form, a mixture of two volatile liquids. Each contributes a partial pressure equal to its mole fraction times its pure vapour pressure, and by Dalton the total is their sum.

For an ideal solution, plot that and every line is straight. The partial pressures are straight lines, and the total pressure is a straight line joining pure A's vapour pressure to pure B's. Look at the plot.
Second form, a non-volatile solute. Only the solvent evaporates, and the relative lowering of vapour pressure, p-degree minus p-s over p-degree, equals the mole fraction of the solute.
Keep the two straight. The solution's pressure itself is p-degree times the solvent mole fraction, but the relative lowering equals the solute mole fraction. Confusing these is the classic slip.
Rearranged for a dilute solution, that same law gives you an unknown molar mass: M two equals w two M one p-degree, over w one times p-degree minus p-s.
And the vapour composition, by Dalton, is y A equals p A over the total. The consequence is worth memorising: the vapour is always richer in the component with the higher pure vapour pressure.
<whisper> One beautiful link back to Henry: Raoult's law is just Henry's law with K sub H equal to p-degree. Same straight line through the origin, different slope.
अब formulas. दो Raoult forms hain, और इस poore subtopic की sabse common galti inhein aapas में mila dena hai.
Pehla form, do volatile liquids ka mixture. Har ek ek partial pressure deta hai equal to uske mole fraction times uske pure vapour pressure, aur Dalton se total unka sum hai.

Ideal solution ke liye, use plot karo aur har line straight hai. Partial pressures straight lines hain, aur total pressure ek straight line hai jo pure A ke vapour pressure ko pure B ke se jodti hai. Plot dekho.
Doosra form, ek non-volatile solute. Sirf solvent evaporate karta hai, aur relative lowering of vapour pressure, p-degree minus p-s over p-degree, equals solute ka mole fraction.
Dono ko alag rakho. Solution ka pressure khud p-degree times solvent mole fraction hai, par relative lowering solute mole fraction ke barabar hai. Inhein confuse karna classic slip hai.
Dilute solution ke liye rearrange karo, aur wahi law tumhe unknown molar mass deta hai: M two equals w two M one p-degree, over w one times p-degree minus p-s.
Aur vapour composition, Dalton se, hai y A equals p A over total. Consequence yaad karne layak hai: vapour hamesha us component mein richer hoti hai jiska pure vapour pressure zyada hai.

board_events.text: Ex 2 (NEET): which shows negative deviation? Ask only: does a new, stronger A-B bond form on mixing?
Acetone + chloroform: chloroform H-bonds to the carbonyl $\Rightarrow$ negative deviation. Answer: that pair.
New H-bond $\Rightarrow$ negative; H-bonds broken $\Rightarrow$ positive; look-alike molecules $\Rightarrow$ ideal.

segments.text: Two examples: one is a clean computation, the other is answered by pure reasoning, no numbers at all.

Example one, board level. Liquids P and Q form an ideal solution. At three hundred kelvin, pure P has vapour pressure one hundred twenty and pure Q seventy-five, both in millimetres of mercury. Mix three moles of P with two moles of Q, and find the total vapour pressure.

The mole fractions are three-fifths, zero point six zero, for P, and zero point four zero for Q. So the partial pressures are zero point six zero times one hundred twenty, which is seventy-two, and zero point four zero times seventy-five, which is thirty.
By Dalton, the total is simply seventy-two plus thirty, one hundred two millimetres of mercury.
Example two needs no arithmetic. The question is which mixture shows a negative deviation. Look at the molecules.
Ask one thing only: does a new, stronger A-B attraction form on mixing? A negative deviation needs A-B stronger than the originals, classically a brand-new hydrogen bond.
Acetone and chloroform is the textbook case: the chloroform hydrogen bonds to the acetone carbonyl, holding molecules back. So that pair is the negative-deviation answer.
<whisper> Lock the rule: a new hydrogen bond on mixing means negative; broken hydrogen bonds mean positive; and look-alike molecules stay ideal.
दो examples: एक clean computation hai, doosra pure reasoning से answer hota hai, बिलकुल numbers के bina.

Example ek, board level. Liquids P aur Q ek ideal solution banate hain. Three hundred kelvin par, pure P ka vapour pressure one hundred twenty aur pure Q ka seventy-five hai, dono millimetres of mercury mein. Three moles P ko two moles Q ke saath mix karo, aur total vapour pressure nikalo.

Mole fractions hain three-fifths, zero point six zero, P ke liye, aur zero point four zero Q ke liye. Toh partial pressures hain zero point six zero times one hundred twenty, jo seventy-two hai, aur zero point four zero times seventy-five, jo thirty hai.
Dalton se, total bas seventy-two plus thirty hai, one hundred two millimetres of mercury.
Example do ko koi arithmetic nahi chahiye. Sawaal ye hai ki kaunsa mixture negative deviation dikhata hai. Molecules dekho.
Sirf ek cheez poochho: kya mixing par ek naya, stronger A-B attraction banta hai? Negative deviation ke liye A-B ko originals se strong hona chahiye, classically ek bilkul naya hydrogen bond.
Acetone aur chloroform textbook case hai: chloroform acetone ke carbonyl se hydrogen bond banata hai, molecules ko rok kar. Toh wo pair negative-deviation ka answer hai.
<whisper> Rule lock करो: mixing पर naya hydrogen bond matlab negative; toote hue hydrogen bonds matlab positive; और look-alike molecules ideal rehte hain.

segments.text: The two marquee examples: pulling a molar mass out of a vapour-pressure drop, and showing why the vapour differs from the liquid.

Example three. Five point four grams of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute go into ninety grams of water, and the vapour pressure falls from twenty-three point eight to twenty-three point four millimetres of mercury. Find the molar mass.

The relative lowering is the drop, zero point four, over twenty-three point eight, which is one point six eight one times ten to the minus two. The moles of water are ninety over eighteen, five point zero.

For a dilute solution the relative lowering is about the moles of solute over moles of solvent, so the solute is that fraction times five point zero, eight point four zero times ten to the minus two moles. Molar mass is five point four grams over that, about sixty-four point three.
Example four shows the liquid and the vapour parting ways. Look at the two vessels.
An ideal mixture of A and B has pure vapour pressures four hundred and one hundred millimetres of mercury, and the liquid is forty percent A. Find the total pressure and the vapour composition.

The partial pressures are zero point four zero times four hundred, one hundred sixty, and zero point six zero times one hundred, sixty. The total is two hundred twenty. So y A is one hundred sixty over two hundred twenty, zero point seven two seven.

So although the liquid is only forty percent A, the vapour is about seventy-three percent A, enriched in the more volatile component. Condense that vapour, boil it again, and A climbs further still. That step-by-step enrichment is exactly how fractional distillation works, and it is precisely what fails at an azeotrope.
दो marquee examples: vapour-pressure drop से molar mass nikalna, और ये dikhana ki vapour liquid से अलग क्यों hai.

Example teen. Five point four grams ka ek non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute ninety grams water mein jata hai, aur vapour pressure twenty-three point eight se twenty-three point four millimetres of mercury tak girta hai. Molar mass nikalo.
Relative lowering hai drop, zero point four, over twenty-three point eight, jo one point six eight one times ten to the minus two hai. Moles of water hain ninety over eighteen, five point zero.

Dilute solution ke liye relative lowering lagbhag moles of solute over moles of solvent hai, toh solute wo fraction times five point zero hai, eight point four zero times ten to the minus two moles. Molar mass hai five point four grams us par, lagbhag sixty-four point three.
Example chaar liquid aur vapour ko alag hote dikhata hai. Do vessels dekho.

Partial pressures hain zero point four zero times four hundred, one hundred sixty, aur zero point six zero times one hundred, sixty. Total hai two hundred twenty. Toh y A hai one hundred sixty over two hundred twenty, zero point seven two seven.

तो haalaanki liquid sirf forty percent A hai, vapour lagbhag seventy-three percent A hai, more volatile component में enriched. उस vapour को condense karo, फिर boil karo, और A aur bhi chadhta hai. वो step-by-step enrichment exactly aise fractional distillation kaam karta hai, और वही एक azeotrope पर fail ho jata hai.

sections.title: Pitfalls and speed tricks for Raoult's law

board_events.text: Check first: can the solute evaporate?
Pitfall: mixing the two forms. Use $p = x\,p^{\circ}$ per volatile component; use relative-lowering only for a non-volatile solute.
Pitfall: solute vs solvent mole fraction. $p_{\text{solution}} = p^{\circ}\,x_{\text{solvent}}$, but $\Delta p / p^{\circ} = x_{\text{solute}}$.
Pitfall: deviation sign reversed. Anchor with acetone + chloroform = negative.
Pitfall: azeotrope mapping flipped. Positive $\to$ minimum-boiling; negative $\to$ maximum-boiling.
Speed: for deviation/azeotrope questions, never compute $-$ reason from hydrogen bonding, broken versus formed.
Speed: the vapour is always richer in the higher-$p^{\circ}$ liquid, which eliminates half the options at once.
Sanity: an ideal mixture's total VP must lie between $p_A^{\circ}$ and $p_B^{\circ}$. Outside that range = an error.

segments.text: Four traps, two speed moves, and a sanity check to close the subtopic.

First trap: mixing the two forms. Use p equals x times p-degree for each volatile component, but use the relative-lowering form only when the solute is non-volatile. Always check first whether the solute can evaporate.

Second trap: solute versus solvent mole fraction. The solution's pressure is p-degree times the solvent mole fraction, but the relative lowering equals the solute mole fraction. Write down which one before you plug in.
Third trap: the deviation sign reversed. Anchor it hard: acetone plus chloroform forms a new hydrogen bond, so it is negative.
Fourth trap: the azeotrope mapping flipped. Positive deviation gives a minimum-boiling azeotrope; negative deviation gives a maximum-boiling one.
Now speed. For any deviation or azeotrope question, never compute. Reason purely from hydrogen bonding: broken on mixing means positive, formed on mixing means negative.
And for vapour-composition questions, remember the vapour is always richer in the higher pure-vapour-pressure liquid. That alone eliminates half the options instantly.
<whisper> Finally, a sanity check: the total vapour pressure of an ideal mixture must lie between the two pure values. If your answer falls outside that range, you have a sign or arithmetic error.
Chaar traps, do speed moves, aur ek sanity check subtopic band karne ke liye.

Pehla trap: do forms ko mila dena. Har volatile component ke liye p equals x times p-degree use karo, par relative-lowering form sirf tab use karo jab solute non-volatile ho. Hamesha pehle check karo ki solute evaporate kar sakta hai ya nahi.

Doosra trap: solute versus solvent mole fraction. Solution ka pressure p-degree times solvent mole fraction hai, par relative lowering solute mole fraction ke barabar hai. Plug karne se pehle likh lo kaunsा wala hai.
Teesra trap: deviation sign ulta. Ise mazbooti se anchor karo: acetone plus chloroform ek naya hydrogen bond banata hai, toh ye negative hai.
Chautha trap: azeotrope mapping ulti. Positive deviation minimum-boiling azeotrope deti hai; negative deviation maximum-boiling.
Ab speed. Kisi bhi deviation ya azeotrope sawaal ke liye, kabhi compute mat karo. Sirf hydrogen bonding se reason karo: mixing par toota matlab positive, mixing par bana matlab negative.
Aur vapour-composition sawaalon ke liye, yaad rakho vapour hamesha higher pure-vapour-pressure liquid mein richer hoti hai. Wahi akela aadhे options turant hata deta hai.

<whisper> Aakhir mein, ek sanity check: ideal mixture ka total vapour pressure dono pure values ke beech mein hona chahiye. Agar tumhara answer us range se bahar girta hai, toh sign ya arithmetic error hai.

board_events.text: The four: relative lowering of VP, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, osmotic pressure.
They depend on HOW MANY solute particles are present, not on what they are.
Picture a baraat dance floor: a hundred guests in red crowd it exactly like a hundred in blue.
The solvent feels only the head-count, so a hundred urea molecules act like a hundred glucose molecules.
That is why colligative measurements find an unknown molar mass: count the effect, back out the particle mass.

segments.text: <curious> Here is the beautiful payoff of the last subtopic: one small vapour-pressure drop quietly controls four different physical properties.
We saw that a non-volatile solute lowers a solvent's vapour pressure. That single lowering drags four properties along with it.
And here is the astonishing part, drawn on the board: none of these four cares what the solute actually is. They care only how many particles are dissolved.
The four are: the relative lowering of vapour pressure, the elevation of boiling point, the depression of freezing point, and osmotic pressure.
Because they are bound to the number of particles, not their identity, we call them colligative properties.

Picture a crowded wedding baraat dance floor. Whether you send in a hundred guests wearing red or a hundred wearing blue, the floor feels equally crowded. The crowding is about the head-count, not the colour.
The solvent behaves exactly like that floor. It feels only the number of foreign particles, so a hundred urea molecules act just like a hundred glucose molecules.
And that is precisely why colligative measurements are such a clever tool for finding an unknown molar mass. Count the particles' effect, and you can back-calculate how heavy each particle is.
<curious> ये raha pichhle subtopic ka khoobsurat payoff: एक chhota vapour-pressure drop chupchap chaar अलग physical properties को control karta hai.
Humne dekha ki ek non-volatile solute solvent ka vapour pressure kam karta hai. Wo akela lowering apne saath chaar properties ko kheench leta hai.
Aur ye rahi astonishing baat, board par bani hui: in chaaron mein se kisi ko parwah nahi ki solute asal mein kya hai. Inhein sirf itni parwah hai ki kitne particles dissolved hain.
Chaar ye hain: relative lowering of vapour pressure, boiling point ka elevation, freezing point ka depression, aur osmotic pressure.
Kyunki ye particles ki number se bandhe hain, unki identity se nahi, inhein colligative properties kehte hain.
Ek crowded wedding baraat dance floor socho. Chahe tum sau red pehne guests bhejo ya sau blue pehne, floor ko barabar crowded lagta hai. Crowding head-count ki baat hai, colour ki nahi.
Solvent bilkul us floor ki tarah behave karta hai. Use sirf foreign particles ki number ka pata chalta hai, toh sau urea molecules bilkul sau glucose molecules ki tarah act karte hain.
और इसीलिए colligative measurements unknown molar mass dhundhne ka itna clever tool hain. Particles ka effect gino, और tum back-calculate kar sakte ho ki har particle kitna bhaari hai.

board_events.text: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
The solute pushed vapour pressure down, so you must heat higher to reach atmospheric $\Rightarrow$ boiling point rises by $\Delta T_b$.
The elevation is proportional to molality: $\Delta T_b = K_b\,m$. $K_b$ belongs to the solvent alone.
Freezing is the mirror image: solute particles block the orderly crystal, so you must cool below the pure freezing point.
So freezing point falls by $\Delta T_f = K_f\,m$: salt on icy roads, glycol antifreeze in radiators.
$K_b$ and $K_f$ depend on the solvent's nature, never on the solute's $-$ the colligative signature.

segments.text: Why does adding a solute raise the boiling point and lower the freezing point? Both trace back to that one vapour-pressure drop. Look at the curves.
The solution's vapour-pressure curve, in red, sits below the pure solvent's, in blue, at every single temperature. Everything follows from that gap.
Start with boiling. A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external, atmospheric pressure.

But the solute has pushed the solution's vapour pressure down. So you must heat it to a higher temperature to claw that pressure back up to atmospheric. The boiling point rises, by an amount we call delta T sub b.
Experiment shows this elevation is proportional to molality: delta T sub b equals K sub b times m. And crucially, K sub b is a property of the solvent alone, not the solute.
Freezing is the mirror image. Solute particles get in the way of the orderly crystal lattice trying to form, so you must cool the solution below the pure freezing point before ice can grow.
So the freezing point falls, by delta T sub f equals K sub f times m. That is why we sprinkle salt on icy hill roads and pour glycol antifreeze into a car radiator.
And notice: both K sub b and K sub f depend only on the solvent's nature, never on the solute's identity. That solvent-only dependence is the true colligative signature.
Solute daalne se boiling point क्यों badhta hai और freezing point क्यों girta hai? दोनों usi एक vapour-pressure drop तक jaate hain. Curves dekho.
Solution ka vapour-pressure curve, red mein, pure solvent ke, blue mein, neeche baithta hai har ek temperature par. Sab kuchh us gap se nikalta hai.
Boiling se shuru karo. Ek liquid tab boil karta hai jab uska vapour pressure external, atmospheric pressure ke barabar ho jata hai.

Par solute ne solution ka vapour pressure neeche push kar diya hai. Toh tumhe ise higher temperature tak garam karna padega us pressure ko wapas atmospheric tak laane ke liye. Boiling point badhta hai, ek amount se jise hum delta T sub b kehte hain.
Experiment dikhata hai ye elevation molality ke proportional hai: delta T sub b equals K sub b times m. Aur khaas baat, K sub b sirf solvent ki property hai, solute ki nahi.

Freezing mirror image hai. Solute particles banne ki koshish kar rahe orderly crystal lattice ke raaste mein aate hain, toh tumhe solution ko pure freezing point ke neeche cool karna padega ice banne se pehle.
Toh freezing point girta hai, delta T sub f equals K sub f times m se. Isiliye hum icy hill roads par salt chhidakte hain aur car radiator mein glycol antifreeze daalte hain.
और dhyan do: dono K sub b aur K sub f sirf solvent की nature par depend karte hain, कभी solute की identity par नहीं. वही solvent-only dependence asli colligative signature hai.
