board_events.text: Separate pure solvent from a solution by a semipermeable membrane $-$ it passes solvent, blocks solute.
Solvent spontaneously flows into the solution to dilute it. That flow is osmosis.
Osmotic pressure $\Pi$ is the extra pressure you must apply to the solution to just stop the inflow.
It is formally the ideal-gas law's twin: $\Pi$ tracks concentration and temperature, just like $p = (n/V)RT$.
Best for macromolecules: a tiny concentration gives a measurable pressure at room temperature (no heating).

segments.text: The fourth property comes from a different but related idea: osmosis. The diagram sets it up.
Separate pure solvent on one side from a solution on the other, using a semipermeable membrane. That membrane lets solvent molecules through but blocks the larger solute.
What happens next is spontaneous. Solvent flows through the membrane into the solution, trying to dilute it. That inflow is osmosis.
You can see the solution column rising as solvent pours in from the pure side.
Now the definition. The osmotic pressure, capital pi, is the extra pressure you must push back on the solution to just stop that inflow.
The law is remarkably clean: pi equals concentration times R times T, which is the moles of solute over volume, times R T.
That is formally the twin of the ideal-gas law. Osmotic pressure tracks concentration and temperature exactly the way pressure tracks n over V and temperature for a gas.

And here is why it is the method of choice for huge molecules like proteins: even a tiny molar concentration gives a comfortably measurable pressure at room temperature, with no heating that might denature them.
चौथा property एक अलग par related idea से aata hai: osmosis. Diagram ise set karta hai.
Ek taraf pure solvent ko doosri taraf ke solution se alag karo, ek semipermeable membrane se. Wo membrane solvent molecules ko jaane deti hai par bade solute ko block karti hai.
Aage jo hota hai wo spontaneous hai. Solvent membrane se hokar solution mein flow karta hai, use dilute karne ki koshish mein. Wo inflow osmosis hai.
Tum solution column ko upar uthta dekh sakte ho jaise pure side se solvent bhar-ta hai.
Ab definition. Osmotic pressure, capital pi, wo extra pressure hai jo tumhe solution par wapas push karna padta hai us inflow ko rokne ke liye.
Law kamaal ka saaf hai: pi equals concentration times R times T, jo moles of solute over volume, times R T hai.
Ye formally ideal-gas law ka twin hai. Osmotic pressure concentration aur temperature ko bilkul waise track karta hai jaise pressure gas ke liye n over V aur temperature ko track karta hai.

और ये rahi wajah ki ye proteins jaise huge molecules के liye method of choice क्यों hai: एक chhoti si molar concentration भी room temperature par comfortably measurable pressure deti hai, बिना kisi heating ke jo unhein denature kar de.

More particles $\Rightarrow$ observed molar mass comes out LOWER than the true value.
Or a solute associates: ethanoic acid pairs into dimers in benzene, giving fewer particles, so $i \lt 1$.
Fewer particles $\Rightarrow$ observed molar mass comes out HIGHER than the true value.
Every colligative formula is patched the same way: multiply by $i$. Get $i$ right and all four fall into line.

segments.text: There is one crucial twist that separates a top scorer from the rest: the count-the-particles logic needs the actual number of particles in solution.
And for electrolytes, that number differs from the number you originally dissolved. The diagram shows both directions.

On the left, dissolve one mole of sodium chloride and you get nearly two moles of ions, sodium and chloride. So the van't Hoff factor i is greater than one, and the colligative effect is bigger than expected.
There is a consequence for molar mass. More particles means a larger measured effect, which makes the back-calculated molar mass come out lower than the true value.
On the right, a solute can instead associate. Ethanoic acid pairs up into dimers in benzene through hydrogen bonding, giving fewer particles than you dissolved, so i is less than one.
That reverses the molar-mass consequence. Fewer particles means a smaller effect, which makes the observed molar mass come out higher than the true value.
The fix is wonderfully uniform. Every colligative formula is patched the same way: just multiply by i.
So get i right, count the real particles, and all four colligative formulas fall neatly into line.
Ek crucial twist hai jo ek top scorer ko baaki se alag karta hai: count-the-particles logic ko solution mein actual particles ki number chahiye.
Aur electrolytes ke liye, wo number us number se alag hai jo tumne originally dissolve kiya tha. Diagram dono directions dikhata hai.
Left par, ek mole sodium chloride dissolve karo aur tumhe lagbhag do moles ions milte hain, sodium aur chloride. Toh van't Hoff factor i one se bada hai, aur colligative effect expected se bada hai.
Molar mass ke liye ek consequence hai. Zyada particles matlab bada measured effect, jo back-calculated molar mass ko true value se neeche le aata hai.
Right par, ek solute iski jagah associate kar sakta hai. Ethanoic acid benzene mein hydrogen bonding se dimers mein pair ho jata hai, dissolve kiye se kam particles deta hai, toh i one se kam hai.
Ye molar-mass consequence ko ulta kar deta hai. Kam particles matlab chhota effect, jo observed molar mass ko true value se upar le aata hai.
Fix बहुत uniform hai. Har colligative formula usi tareeke se patch hota hai: bas i se multiply karo.
Toh i sahi karo, real particles gino, aur chaaron colligative formulas saaf line mein aa jaate hain.

board_events.text: Four formulas, one correction factor

board_events.latex: i = \dfrac{\text{normal molar mass}}{\text{observed molar mass}} = \dfrac{\text{observed property}}{\text{calculated property}}

board_events.text: Molality for $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$; molarity for $\Pi$. Mixing them up is the classic blunder.

segments.text: Here is the whole colligative toolkit on one board. Four formulas, and a single correction factor stitched through all of them.
Boiling-point elevation is i times K sub b times molality. Freezing-point depression is i times K sub f times molality. Same shape, different solvent constant.
Osmotic pressure is i times concentration times R times T, where R is zero point zero eight two one litre-atmosphere per kelvin per mole.
Now the trap that loses marks, drawn on the board. The boiling and freezing shifts use molality; osmotic pressure uses molarity. Never swap them.
To find a molar mass, rearrange: M two equals K sub f times w two times one thousand, over delta T sub f times w one; or equally w two R T over pi V from the osmotic route.
The van't Hoff factor itself is the normal molar mass over the observed, which equals the observed colligative effect over the calculated one.
And to reach the degree of change: for dissociation into n particles, i equals one plus n minus one, times alpha. For association, i equals one plus, one over n minus one, times alpha.
<whisper> Burn in the one rule that saves marks: molality for the two temperature shifts, molarity for osmotic pressure.
Ye raha poora colligative toolkit ek board par. Chaar formulas, aur ek single correction factor sab mein piroya hua.

segments.text: Two examples: the first is a clean plug-in, the second you solve just by counting particles.
Example one, board level. Eighteen grams of glucose, molar mass one hundred eighty, dissolved in five hundred grams of water, with K sub b zero point five two. Find the boiling point.

The molality is eighteen over one hundred eighty, all over zero point five kilograms, which is zero point two zero. So delta T sub b is zero point five two times zero point two zero, which is zero point one zero four kelvin.

Glucose is a non-electrolyte, so i is one. The boiling point is three seventy-three point one five plus zero point one zero four, which is three seventy-three point two five kelvin. Remember you add delta T sub b, because boiling point rises.
Example two is pure reasoning. Look at the bars.

Four solutions, each zero point one molal: glucose, sodium chloride, calcium chloride, and potassium sulphate. Order them by increasing freezing point, and do not compute anything. Just count the van't Hoff i.
The values are: glucose one, sodium chloride two, calcium chloride three, potassium sulphate three. More particles means a larger depression, which means a lower freezing point.
So increasing freezing point runs: calcium chloride and potassium sulphate lowest, then sodium chloride, then glucose highest. Glucose, with the fewest particles, always sits at the top.

segments.text: The two marquee numericals: a protein molar mass from osmosis, and a van't Hoff factor turned into a degree of dissociation.

Example three. Two point one zero grams of a protein sit in two hundred fifty millilitres of solution, and the osmotic pressure at three hundred kelvin is seven point zero times ten to the minus three atmosphere. Find the molar mass.

Rearrange the osmotic law: M two equals w two R T over pi V. That is two point one zero times zero point zero eight two one times three hundred, all over seven point zero times ten to the minus three, times zero point two five zero.

The top is fifty-one point seven two, the bottom is one point seven five times ten to the minus three, so the molar mass is about two point nine six times ten to the fourth, near thirty thousand. A tiny pressure still pins down a huge molecule.
Example four brings in the van't Hoff factor. Look at the two depressions on the board.

One point zero gram of a weak monobasic acid, molar mass one hundred, in one hundred grams of water, gives an observed freezing-point depression of zero point two one seven kelvin, with K sub f one point eight six.

The molality is zero point one zero, so the expected depression, with no dissociation, is one point eight six times zero point one zero, which is zero point one eight six. The van't Hoff factor is the observed over the calculated: zero point two one seven over zero point one eight six, which is one point one six seven.

The acid splits into two particles, hydrogen and A-minus, so i equals one plus alpha. That gives alpha equals zero point one six seven, about sixteen point seven percent dissociated, exactly what we expect from a weak acid.

sections.title: Pitfalls and speed tricks for colligative properties

board_events.text: Settle i first, and mind molality vs molarity
Pitfall: forgetting van't Hoff i for electrolytes. Always multiply by i (the ion count for strong electrolytes).
Pitfall: molality vs molarity. $\Delta T_b$ and $\Delta T_f$ take molality; $\Pi = CRT$ takes molarity.
Pitfall: the sign of $\Delta T$. BP = pure BP + $\Delta T_b$; FP = pure FP $-$ $\Delta T_f$.
Pitfall: association vs dissociation direction. Dissociation $\Rightarrow i \gt 1$, observed M lower; association $\Rightarrow i \lt 1$, observed M higher.
Speed: for highest/lowest BP or FP among equimolal solutions, never compute $-$ just rank i (count the ions).
Sanity: a strong electrolyte's i lies between 1 and its ion count; an associating solute's i between 0 and 1.
More pieces, more effect: every colligative property counts particles, so always settle i first.

segments.text: Four traps, a speed move, and a sanity check to close the subtopic and the chapter's numericals.

First trap, and the most common lost mark: forgetting the van't Hoff factor for electrolytes. Always multiply by i, which is the ion count for a strong electrolyte, in delta T sub b, delta T sub f, and pi.
Second trap: molality versus molarity. The boiling and freezing shifts take molality; osmotic pressure, pi equals C R T, takes molarity. Check which before substituting.

Third trap: the sign of delta T. The boiling point is the pure value plus delta T sub b; the freezing point is the pure value minus delta T sub f. Adding delta T sub f to the freezing point is a frequent slip.

Fourth trap: the association versus dissociation direction. Dissociation gives i greater than one and an observed molar mass that is lower; association gives i less than one and an observed molar mass that is higher.
Now the speed move. For highest or lowest boiling or freezing point among equimolal solutions, never compute. Just rank the van't Hoff i by counting the ions.
And a sanity check: a strong electrolyte's i should land between one and its maximum ion count, while an associating solute's i sits between zero and one. An i outside those bounds means an error.
<whisper> One line ties the whole subtopic together: more pieces, more effect. Every colligative property counts particles, so always settle i first.
Chaar traps, ek speed move, aur ek sanity check subtopic aur chapter ke numericals band karne ke liye.

Pehla trap, aur sabse common lost mark: electrolytes ke liye van't Hoff factor bhoolna. Hamesha i se multiply karo, jo ek strong electrolyte ke liye ion count hai, delta T sub b, delta T sub f, aur pi mein.
Doosra trap: molality versus molarity. Boiling aur freezing shifts molality lete hain; osmotic pressure, pi equals C R T, molarity leta hai. Substitute karne se pehle check karo kaunsा wala hai.
Teesra trap: delta T ka sign. Boiling point pure value plus delta T sub b hai; freezing point pure value minus delta T sub f hai. Freezing point mein delta T sub f add karna ek frequent slip hai.
Chautha trap: association versus dissociation direction. Dissociation deta hai i one se bada aur observed molar mass lower; association deta hai i one se kam aur observed molar mass higher.
Ab speed move. Equimolal solutions mein highest ya lowest boiling ya freezing point ke liye, kabhi compute mat karo. Bas van't Hoff i ko ions gin kar rank karo.

Aur ek sanity check: ek strong electrolyte ka i one aur uske maximum ion count ke beech hona chahiye, jabki ek associating solute ka i zero aur one ke beech baithta hai. In bounds se bahar i matlab ek error.

segments.text: Let us pull the whole chapter onto one board, subtopic by subtopic, so the backbone formulas sit together.

From concentration: molarity is moles per litre of solution, molality is moles per kilogram of solvent, and from a mass percentage with density, molarity is ten times mass percent times density, over the molar mass.
From Henry's law: p equals K sub H times x, so x is p over K sub H, and to move between pressures the ratio s one over s two equals p one over p two.

From Raoult's law: the total pressure of a volatile mixture is the sum of each mole fraction times its pure vapour pressure, and for a non-volatile solute the relative lowering equals the solute mole fraction.
From colligative properties: boiling-point elevation is i K sub b m, freezing-point depression is i K sub f m, and osmotic pressure is i C R T.
And the van't Hoff factor: for dissociation, i is one plus n minus one times alpha; for association, i is one plus, one over n minus one, times alpha.
Now step back and see the whole map. Five subtopics, each flowing into the next.

Trace the threads. Molality feeds every colligative formula. Mole fraction feeds both Raoult and Henry. And Raoult's law is simply Henry's law with K sub H equal to p-degree. That is the entire chapter in one breath.

Concentration se: molarity hai moles per litre of solution, molality hai moles per kilogram of solvent, aur mass percentage aur density se, molarity hai ten times mass percent times density, over molar mass.
Henry's law se: p equals K sub H times x, toh x hai p over K sub H, aur pressures ke beech jaane ke liye ratio s one over s two equals p one over p two.

Raoult's law se: ek volatile mixture ka total pressure hai har mole fraction times uske pure vapour pressure ka sum, aur ek non-volatile solute ke liye relative lowering solute mole fraction ke barabar hai.
Colligative properties se: boiling-point elevation hai i K sub b m, freezing-point depression hai i K sub f m, aur osmotic pressure hai i C R T.
Aur van't Hoff factor: dissociation ke liye, i hai one plus n minus one times alpha; association ke liye, i hai one plus, one over n minus one, times alpha.
Ab peeche hat kar poora map dekho. Paanch subtopics, har ek agle mein flow karta hua.
